subject: WAIC and loo for a model with measurement error in the predictors

messages.author: 5d67cef991a09367
messages.subject: WAIC and loo for a model with measurement error in the predictors
parts:
Hello group,

I'm fitting a model where one of the predictors is measured several times per each observation of the outcome, so I decided to include this as measurement error, estimating the mean and SE of the mean of the predictor for each observation of the outcome, and then building a model for that. I'd also like to compare models, so I was wondering if I could just use WAIC on the log probability function of the outcome given covariates?
Secondly, I was wondering if summarizing the distribution of predictor values for each observation of the outcome as a mean and SE is the right way to go here.

Thank for any advice you can provide on this,

Tada

On Monday, February 6, 2017 at 10:40:32 PM UTC+2, Tadaishi Yatabe wrote:
I'm fitting a model where one of the predictors is measured several times per each observation of the outcome, so I decided to include this as measurement error, estimating the mean and SE of the mean of the predictor for each observation of the outcome, and then building a model for that. I'd also like to compare models, so I was wondering if I could just use WAIC on the log probability function of the outcome given covariates?

Instead of WAIC I recommend PSIS-LOO (paper http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-016-9696-4, preprint http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.04544)
If you are interested only in the predictive performance of your model for the outcomes, then you can use loo just for them. If you are interested also how good your model is for measurement error you can use loo for that, too.
Secondly, I was wondering if summarizing the distribution of predictor values for each observation of the outcome as a mean and SE is the right way to go here.

It is right way if it's a good model. You could use predictive checking and loo to check that.

Aki

Thank for any advice you can provide on this,

Tada

When you say "If you are interested only in the predictive performance of your model for the outcomes, then you can use loo just for them" you mean just using the log-likelihood of the outcomes for the computation of PSIS-LOO?

Related to the above, when I trythe psis-loo from the loo package (thank for that too!), and I noticed I have a fair chunk of problematic k estimates (about 40% between 0.5 and 1, and 40% >1), so I think I'm in trouble. I wonder if it has anything to do with the way I'm defining my loglik, where besides the likelihood of the observed outcomes, I'm also adding the likelihoods of the observed predictors: 


for (i in 1:N){
log_lik[i] = neg_binomial_2_lpmf( mort[i] | lambda[i] , theta )
              +normal_lpdf( Ten[i] | Ten_est[i] , Tense[i] )
              +normal_lpdf( pox[i] | pox_est[i] , poxse[i] )
              +normal_lpdf( PRV[i] | PRV_est[i] , PRVse[i] )
              +normal_lpdf( cyst[i] | cyst_est[i] , cystse[i])
              +normal_lpdf( Des[i] | Des_est[i] , Desse[i])
              +normal_lpdf( AGD[i] | AGD_est[i] , AGDse[i]);
}

Thanks again Aki,

Tada

On Thursday, February 9, 2017 at 9:04:49 PM UTC+2, Tadaishi Yatabe wrote:
Related to the above, when I trythe psis-loo from the loo package (thank for that too!), and I noticed I have a fair chunk of problematic k estimates (about 40% between 0.5 and 1, and 40% >1), so I think I'm in trouble.

Yes, the full posterior and leave-one-out posterior are too different (good that we a way to check this). If you want to make M-open type predictive performance estimate, I recommend using k-fold cross-validation.
I wonder if it has anything to do with the way I'm defining my loglik, where besides the likelihood of the observed outcomes, I'm also adding the likelihoods of the observed predictors:

It is possible that you could get high k values also if you have just "neg_binomial_2_lpmf( mort[i] | lambda[i] , theta )" there. I recommend to check this, because in that case large number of high k values indicate a problem in your model.
You can also make separate LOO for each the covariate prediction models. Maybe you have outliers, normal distribution has too thin tails and you should switch to something more robust like Student's t.
On the other hand, it is possible that you get high k values because summing many terms. As discussed also here https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.0264,6 importance sampling is more likely to fail when the number of dimensions increase.

Aki

for (i in 1:N){
log_lik[i] = neg_binomial_2_lpmf( mort[i] | lambda[i] , theta )
              +normal_lpdf( Ten[i] | Ten_est[i] , Tense[i] )
              +normal_lpdf( pox[i] | pox_est[i] , poxse[i] )
              +normal_lpdf( PRV[i] | PRV_est[i] , PRVse[i] )
              +normal_lpdf( cyst[i] | cyst_est[i] , cystse[i])
              +normal_lpdf( Des[i] | Des_est[i] , Desse[i])
              +normal_lpdf( AGD[i] | AGD_est[i] , AGDse[i]);
}

Thanks again Aki,

Tada
